title: The full text of the constitution is printed in the Herald
body: The College Heights Herald of 7 April 1966 printed the constitution of the Associated Students in full, five columns across a page, six days after President Kelly Thompson approved it and nineteen days before the ratification vote. It is the copy TopSCHOLAR holds, and the only complete text of the founding framework in the archive.
src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, printed in the College Heights Herald, 7 Apr 1966

title: The first Congress of Associated Students is seated with twenty-five members
body: The roster kept in the President's Office lists the twenty-five people elected in May 1966 with the seat each held: four Associated Students officers, nine class seats across the senior, junior and sophomore councils, two Interfraternity and two Panhellenic representatives, two men's residence hall representatives and one women's, one representative each for professional and honorary fraternities, departmental clubs and general college clubs, and two campus-wide representatives at large. No freshman seats appear; the constitution gave the freshman council three.

title: A constitutional amendment on the treasurer's qualifications goes on the spring ballot
body: The ballot used in the spring 1968 election carried a constitutional amendment to revise the qualifications for treasurer, alongside the cheerleader election and a student fee question. The results memo of 3 May 1968 reports the offices only, so the archive does not record how the amendment fared.

title: Congress votes 18 to 1 to re-examine the constitution
body: The Herald reported that in the previous week's meeting the Congress of Associated Students voted 18 to one for a resolution by general clubs representative Kent Gildersleeve to form a committee to revise the constitution. Gildersleeve argued that clubs and professional and service fraternities with memberships as large as many Greek organisations had no direct representative in Congress while the Panhellenic and Interfraternity Councils had two each, and said he was not being anti-Greek but wanted more students able to take part. President Bill Straeffer called the resolution excellent, said the officers had known on taking office that the existing constitution was barely adequate, called its wording ambiguous, and said one representative then stood for about forty clubs. Sophomore class president Steve Stephens cast the single vote against, saying the matter had been brought up hurriedly and that Congress had not been told what specifically needed changing.

title: The Herald backs revision and warns against a Greek-independent fight
body: An editorial headed that constitution revision could mean progress called the step long overdue, said the existing constitution contained far too many ambiguities and did not give equal representation to all groups and individuals, urged the committee to include provisions for more direct participation by all students, and argued the Student Affairs Board should be reorganised so that students had the voting majority. It closed by warning that treating equal representation in Congress as a power struggle between Greeks and independents could hinder the development of a workable and fair student government.

title: The revision committee reports its progress to Congress
body: A report on revision progress was submitted to the Associated Students Congress, five weeks before the 8 May deadline the February resolution had set.

title: The revision committee calls a meeting on representation
body: The Associated Students revision committee called a meeting on representation, putting the apportionment of Congress seats directly on the table. The following week's issue reported the revision group discussing proposals.

title: Congress sets a budget vote and drops the music survey question
body: The Herald reported that a vote on the budget was set for the following week in the Associated Students Congress, the power the constitution gave Congress over the money. The same issue reported Congress dropping discussion of the validity of its music preference survey.

title: Congress prepares to act on a new constitution
body: Rick Neumayer reported that the Associated Student Government was preparing to act on a new constitution, the product of the revision committee formed the previous February.

title: Work halts on the constitution
body: The Herald of 13 January 1970 carried an item headed that work had halted on the constitution, nine weeks after the draft was sent back for study. The same issue reported the Congress joining the fight against the proposed state superboard and Paul Gerard seeking the right to vote on the Board of Regents.

title: Congress returns to the constitution changes
body: The Herald announced that the Associated Student Congress would discuss constitution changes. A week later Paul Hightower reported a committee constituting efforts to change the constitution, and the issue of 20 February reported the Associated Student Government enlarging its committees.

title: Voting on the amendments runs until four o'clock
body: Tom Todd reported that voting continued until 4 p.m. for cheerleaders and amendments, the ballot on which the four constitutional changes approved by Congress on 24 April were put to the student body. The archive holds no report of the result.

title: Congress recognises United Black Students
body: Paul Hightower reported that the Associated Students had okayed United Black Students. Under Article III, Section 7e of the 1966 constitution, ruling on petitions from student organisations seeking University recognition, by a two-thirds affirmative vote, was one of the powers reserved to Congress.

title: ASC Bill No. 3 creates an Environmental Commission
body: Vice president David Porter sent WKU faculty members a memo about Associated Student Congress Bill No. 3, establishing an Environmental Commission, with the bill attached. It is the earliest numbered bill of the Congress held in the archive; the legislation index begins at 1991-92.
src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Environmental Commission, David Porter, 15 May 1970

title: Congress fails to make quorum and key business is delayed
body: Clark Hanes reported in the Herald that a failure to maintain a quorum delayed action on key issues before the Associated Student Congress. It is the first quorum failure recorded in this archive for the decade.

title: Student paper reports the Regents slashed an Academic Council proposal
body: Rick Neumayer reported in the student paper Expatriate that the Board of Regents had slashed an Academic Council proposal. The archive does not hold the article's text, so what was cut is not established. Five days earlier the Herald had reported the Regents seating eight students on the Council.

title: Congress resolution urges an inquiry into the police department
body: The Herald reported an Associated Students resolution urging a probe of the police department. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the resolution's subject and its outcome are not established.

title: A quorum amendment goes on the ballot with six Academic Council seats
body: Voters decided an Associated Student Congress constitutional quorum question at the Tuesday election of 6 October 1970, on the same ballot as six Academic Council seats. The Herald's preview in the same issue reported a primary turnout of 8.9 per cent. The result of the quorum question is not recorded in this archive.

title: Congress urges repeal of women's hours
body: Paul Hightower reported that the Associated Student Congress had urged repeal of women's hours. Congress mapped strategy for the dorm issues a week later, a committee drafted steps toward abolishing hours on 10 November, and dean of student affairs Charles Keown addressed Congress on hours in November.

title: The constitution referendum is set without the election unit's help
body: David Sutherland reported that the constitution referendum had been set without help from the election unit, four days after the Herald reported the document sparking controversy.

title: Constitution passes with 2,094 students voting
body: The Herald reported that the constitution had passed and that 2,094 students voted. Congress had endorsed the document on 20 November. A committee reopened the study of Associated Student constitutions in January 1971 and revision continued into 1972; the archive does not record why the December document did not settle the question.

title: The course survey is postponed to the autumn
body: The Herald reported that the survey of courses had been postponed until the fall under the heading 'Re-Evaluation'. The previous July the paper had reported that teacher evaluation showed an increase in participation.

title: Congress approves its committees for the year
body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students had approved committees. Four weeks later the Legal Rights Committee set out its programmes in the paper.

title: Constitution Revision Committee releases its findings
body: Travis Witt reported that the Constitution Revision Committee had released its findings. The 1972 Talisman recorded that the committee presented President Dero Downing with guidelines for a new constitution that autumn, and Carter Pence reported on 3 December that the committee was readying the new document.

title: An amendment passes in the autumn balloting
body: The Herald reported that an amendment passed easily in the same balloting that elected Hugh Campbell freshman president. The archive does not hold the article's text, so what the amendment changed is not established.

title: Associated Students asks a Herald reporter to leave
body: Roger Miller reported that the Associated Students had asked a reporter to leave. Congress passed a bill to open its meetings thirteen months later, in March 1973.

title: Congress approves the new constitution
body: The Herald reported that Congress had approved the new constitution, nine days after it voted on the executive branch section and the paper printed that section's full text.

title: Students ratify the new Associated Students constitution
body: Roger Miller reported that students had given their approval to the new Associated Students constitution, voted on 29 and 30 March. The document renamed the body Associated Student Government, created two vice presidencies and replaced special-interest seats with representation from the academic colleges from 1972-73.

title: A board rules that Kim Weaver can seek ASG office
body: John Lucas reported that a board had ruled Kim Weaver could seek Associated Student Government office. The archive does not hold the article's text, so which board ruled and on what ground is not established.

title: The Judicial Council declines to act
body: Elaine Ayers reported that the Judicial Council had declined to act. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the matter before the council is not established. John Lyne's account of the previous year had described the Judicial Council as struggling for authority.

title: Congress college elections are partly voided after a ballot discrepancy
body: A count of the 1972 Homecoming Queen election showed a difference of 275 between ballots cast and voters recorded. ASG's Rules and Elections Committee called for a re-election of the queen and declared only the Who's Who vote and the Congress elections for three colleges valid. The re-vote was held on the Friday before Homecoming Day and was disrupted for over an hour when a group of Black students blocked the polls; the polls reopened shortly before 10 a.m. after their leaders met ASG officers.

title: Congress votes to appeal a Student Affairs decision
body: Carter Pence reported that the ASG Congress had voted to appeal a decision of the office of Student Affairs. The archive does not hold the article's text, so the decision appealed and the outcome are not established.

title: ASG resubmits a bill of rights
body: Carter Pence reported that ASG had resubmitted its bill of rights. John Lyne's 1971 account had described the drafting of a student code of rights as part of the constitutional effort. The archive does not record what became of the resubmitted document.

title: Fiorella proposes a $3.50 head fee increase
body: Al Cross reported activities vice president Mike Fiorella proposing a $3.50 increase in the head fee to improve the quality of entertainment. Congress voted on 24 April to put the increase to a student referendum, and the Herald reported the vote set for 2 May 1973.

title: Congress passes a bill to open its meetings
body: Steven Russell reported that ASG had passed a bill to open its meetings, thirteen months after the Associated Students asked a Herald reporter to leave.

title: Reginald Glass asks for minority representation
body: Jerry Elam reported that Reginald Glass had asked for minority representation. Glass, the ASG representative from the Graduate College and vice president of the body in 1971-72, had sought better representation for minority groups in student government and on the Academic Council; he said the lack of Black and foreign students in these groups harmed both the minorities and the University. He resigned his Congress seat in protest that December.
src_label: Herald 53:12, 9 Oct 1973; 1974 Talisman, Associated Student Government, p. 57

title: Glenn Jackson introduces the reorganization bill
body: Carl Clayworth reported that administrative vice president Glenn Jackson had introduced a bill to reorganize ASG. Congress approved it, abolishing the committee system and folding all programmes into student affairs and academic affairs, each under an area chairman, with projects assigned by the president subject to Congress approval. The Activities, Rules and Elections, and Legislative Research Committees were kept. The Herald reported ASG acting to implement the revamping on 15 February 1974.

title: Amendment issues on the autumn ballot
body: The Herald reported that amendment issues highlighted the autumn balloting. The archive does not hold the article's text, so what the amendments proposed and whether they carried are not established.

title: ASG seeks more student votes on the Academic Council
body: Scott Johnston reported that ASG was seeking more votes on the Academic Council. ASG drew up a resolution for the Council's Rules Committee asking for three more student votes and sought voting status for its three executive officers, on the ground that students without a declared major were not represented through a college. The Council then had two representatives from each of seven colleges, half of them voting, out of 40 votes.
src_label: Herald 50:7, 20 Sep 1974; 1975 Talisman, Associated Student Government

title: A bill seeks a financial report from ASG
body: Jim Reynolds reported a bill seeking an ASG financial report. In February 1975 the Herald reported that ASG funds were dwindling and that Congress had heard the treasurer's explanation of the budget.

title: ASG votes to study its own effectiveness
body: Betsy Leake reported that ASG would study its own effectiveness. Four days later the paper reported that a report showed ASG funds were dwindling, and on 7 February that financial difficulties might force the organisation to drop its entertainment duties.

title: An ASG resolution becomes University policy through the Regents
body: The academic complaint system became University policy when the Board of Regents approved it in January 1975, four months after ASG passed a resolution asking that the complaint system be accelerated. A second ASG resolution, asking that incompletes not be counted in the computation of grade point averages, also reached the regents and was approved. The day of the January approval is not given in the source.

title: A Congress member counts the empty seats
body: In a letter printed in the Herald of 4 October 1974, Congress member Marc Levy wrote that he had hoped the year's meetings would differ from the previous year's invisible congress. He reported a roll call at the meeting of 1 October 1974 showing a good number of people missing, and said three of the four committee reports were delivered by president Jeff Consolo because of absences. Consolo said people had contacted him about filling vacancies on the congress.
src_label: 1975 Talisman, Associated Student Government, quoting the College Heights Herald of 4 Oct 1974

title: A Congress resolution and petition produce a presidential committee on housing
body: After weeks of debate that included an ASG resolution and a committee petition requesting an open visitation policy, President Dero Downing appointed a thirteen-member committee of eight faculty members and five students to study overall university housing policies. The 1973 Talisman does not date the appointment.

title: Constitutional abuses alleged against the activities vice president
body: The Herald's index for the issue of 3 October 1975 lists an article by Jay Wethington and Roger Harris headlined "Constitutional Abuses Alleged Against Rick Kelley", ASG's activities vice president. The archive holds the index entry only, not the article's account of what was alleged, and no source found records a finding. Kelley was re-elected activities vice president in April 1976, defeating Robert Tackett 705 to 496.
src_label: College Heights Herald 51:11, 3 Oct 1975; result in Herald 51:53, 9 Apr 1976

title: Six congressmen open impeachment proceedings against the Judicial Council chairman
body: On 16 March 1976 impeachment proceedings were initiated by six congressmen, on a motion by congress member Marc Levy, to investigate Gerard Faulk's handling of two cases sent to the Judicial Council he chaired. One concerned his action on a report carrying Tom Blair's allegation that president Steve Henry had obstructed the function of an advisory intramurals committee; the other was the misuse-of-funds charge Levy had brought against treasurer David Payne the previous semester. Congress postponed its decision a week later after members questioned the impeachment procedures.

title: Colleagues say the activities vice president is neglecting his duties
body: The Herald reported that ASG members said activities vice president David Carwell was not doing the job Western paid him $800 a year to do, citing missed ASG meetings, missed committee meetings and unkept office hours. Carwell had missed five ASG meetings; under the constitution a member was warned after four absences and could be voted out after six. President Steve Thornton said one more absence would take Carwell before the executive council, that the executive committee could excuse absences for extenuating circumstances, and that if it did not accept his excuses the question would go to Congress for a vote on whether he could remain in ASG. Carwell defended his record, saying his record showed he was doing a good job. The archive holds no report of a removal vote, and he was still activities vice president at the first meeting of the spring semester in January 1979.
src_label: College Heights Herald 54:30, 7 Dec 1978; still in office in 54:33, 18 Jan 1979

title: Students ratify the constitution revision 1,343 to 170; ten of 24 at-large seats filled
body: The revision of the ASG constitution was ratified by students, 1,343 to 170, at the general election. Ten representatives-at-large were chosen. The College of Education Academic Council seat drew no candidates, and neither did the second graduate college seat or its Academic Council seat; most college races were unopposed. Turnout was 1,725, against 1,097 in the 1978 election. A defeated candidate for senior class vice president called for a recount and the president said ASG would go back to the ballots to check the count.

title: The new Congress refuses to short-circuit its own two-reading rule
body: At the first meeting of the Congress elected in April 1980, presided over by President Steve Fuller, Resolution 80-1 on permission for room inspection had its first reading. A motion to suspend the rules so the resolution could be voted on immediately was defeated 20-8 with one abstention. Later in the same meeting the rules were suspended for a different resolution, which passed unanimously. Fuller made two appointments to seats on Congress and a University Center Board representative was nominated from the floor and appointed unanimously.

title: The dean criticises a resolution and members leave before the vote
body: Diane Comer reported in the Herald that Dean of Student Affairs Charles Keown criticised an Associated Student Government resolution and that members left before the vote was taken. The dean of student affairs was the constitutional adviser to ASG.

title: Congress amends its constitution clause by clause
body: At the meeting of 1 December 1981, presided over by President Marcel Bush with five members absent, a resolution carrying constitutional amendments was read for the third time and voted on clause by clause. The clause on the grade-point requirement failed. Clauses passed requiring the president to have one semester's experience, requiring the treasurer to have six hours of accounting, giving the secretary supervision of the office secretaries, changing a deadline in the impeachment article, and amending the judicial article, including a change from one member to five. A clause of the membership article was amended from the floor by Donna Bristow to delete its final sentence.

title: Congress elects a new administrative vice-president by secret ballot
body: Two weeks after Marcel Bush resigned the presidency, Congress met under President David Payne and took nominations for administrative vice-president. Margaret Ragan and Doug Hill were nominated, gave speeches, and a secret ballot was taken; Ragan won. Roll call recorded a single absence, which the secretary announced was a record for the year. A dispute over whether the constitution or the student handbook governed the proceeding was settled in favour of the handbook.

title: Payne's residency appeal fails and a student regent election is set
body: The Herald of 26 January 1982 reported that David Payne's appeal against the rejection of his in-state residency request had failed and that a regent election had been set. A week earlier Kevin Francke had reported that Payne would appeal. The ASG constitution made the president the student member of the Board of Regents except where the president was a non-resident of Kentucky, in which case a special election for a student regent was required.

title: The judicial appointments are criticised in print
body: One week after the council was appointed, the Herald of 4 February 1982 carried a news story by Kevin Francke headlined that the judicial appointments had been criticised, alongside a letter from Paul Deom headlined that a former Judicial Council member was irked. The Herald of 18 February carried a further letter from Winston Stevenson defending Deom, and a Francke story reporting that a group would speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf.

title: Two members appointed to Congress mid-year
body: At the meeting of 9 February 1982, under President David Payne, a resolution had its second reading and passed, and two appointments were made to Congress and approved. The public affairs vice-president announced a speakers bureau whose stated purposes were to familiarise students with ASG, to encourage people to run, and to encourage people to vote.

title: A joke resolution almost passes
body: The Herald of 15 April 1982, the issue that reported the general election results voided, also carried a story by Kevin Francke headlined that a joke resolution had almost passed the Associated Student Government, and a piece by Robert Pillow headlined that ASG would not win an award for organization.

title: The new Congress restructures its committees and writes an absence rule
body: At the organising meeting of 29 April 1982, President Margaret Ragan carried a restructuring that placed the On-Campus, Off-Campus, Student Opinion Poll, Minority Affairs and International Students committees under the Student Affairs Committee, renamed the Communications Committee the Public Relations Committee, and dissolved the Complaints and Suggestions Committee. Treasurer Kelly Cook carried two by-law amendments on absence, one making three unexcused committee absences equal to one unexcused Congress absence. Congress approved a block of appointments to on-campus, off-campus, at-large and college representative seats, and the newly appointed members were sworn in by the chairman of the Judicial Council. Ragan's eight committee chairmen were approved in the same sitting.

title: Two graduate seats reported vacant as the constitutional revision has its first reading
body: At the meeting of 1 March 1983, chaired by Public Affairs Vice-President Kerrie Stewart with seven members absent by name, Secretary Susan Albert announced two openings on Congress: Graduate College Representative and Graduate College Alternate. Congress appointed Lee Ann Turner to the vacant Ogden College Representative seat on a motion from the floor. The ad hoc Constitutional Revision Committee, chaired by Albert, brought the proposed changes for their first reading.

title: The constitutional revision is voted through clause by clause
body: At the meeting of 15 March 1983, chaired by Administrative Vice-President Jack Smith with three members absent, the proposed changes to the constitution, pages one to eight, had their second reading. Happy Chandler moved to limit debate to five minutes on each proposed change and the motion carried. Some thirty-six clauses were then voted on individually, covering the preamble and the executive, legislative and membership articles; one clause failed and the rest passed. Rex Hurt moved to table the remaining changes until the following Tuesday. Secretary Susan Albert announced three openings on Congress that night: Graduate College Representative, Graduate College Alternate and Representative-At-Large.

title: The Herald finds ASG, the Center Board and Interhall Council overlapping
body: Mark Edelen reported in the Herald that the Associated Student Government, the University Center Board and Interhall Council overlapped in their duties. ASG's entertainment programming had passed to the University Center Board before this block began.

title: Four unexcused absences recorded by name
body: The minutes of 2 April 1985, at a meeting chaired by Administrative Vice-President Julie Lippert, list four members absent without excuse by name. Nine committees reported, and the Legislative Research Committee reported that two resolutions were in order, which both then passed. Congress appointed a Book Exchanger committee chairman and moved to form an ad hoc committee on how the bookstore stored books.

title: The last meeting of the Smith Congress
body: At the final meeting of the 1984-85 Congress on 9 April 1985, President Jack Smith congratulated the incoming executive officers and the minutes recorded no absences. A resolution had its first reading, a motion to suspend the rules and vote immediately passed, and the resolution passed. Executive Council awards were given.

title: A Financial Advisory Council replaces the Finance Committee
body: Two weeks after abolishing the Finance Committee, Congress passed Bill 85-2-F creating a Financial Advisory Council of the four class presidents, the Business College representative and alternate, and the treasurer, chaired by the Business College representative and holding unlimited access to Congress's financial records. It could be called into session by its chairman, a majority of the council or Congress whenever a discrepancy in expenditure arose. Authored by the Legislative Research Committee, it passed 26-4 on its second reading.
src_label: SGA Bill 85-2-F, Formation of Financial Advisory Council

title: Congress declines to lower its own grade requirement
body: Bill 85-5-F would have put to the student body a constitutional amendment cutting the grade-point requirement for a member of Congress from 2.25 to 2.0, arguing that a student with a 2.0 was not on academic probation and could graduate, play sport and join a fraternity. Its six authors included Greg Elder and Tim Todd. On its second reading on 29 October 1985 it failed, the division recorded as 16-14.
src_label: SGA Bill 85-5-F, Reduction of Grade Point Average for Congress Members

title: Congress refuses to let absent authors vote
body: Bill 86-8-S would have amended the by-laws to let Congress members who authored or sponsored pending legislation vote in absentia by written approval and signature filed with the recording secretary and read out at the meeting. Its first premise was that Congress members could vote only if they were present. It failed 4-28 on its second reading.

title: A congress race decided by eight votes
body: The Herald reported that the top race in the October Associated Student Government elections had been decided by only eight votes. The same issue reported Congress defeating a bill that would have made the athletic fee optional.

title: One member wrote most of the congress's bills
body: Lisa Jessie reported that a single member, Bill Schilling, wrote most of the bills coming before Congress. The surviving index preserves the headline but not the article text, so the number of bills is not recorded here.
src_label: Herald 62:29, 11 Dec 1986, "One Associated Student Government Member Writes Most of Congress Bills"

title: Todd beats Elder in an election re-run
body: Leigh Eagleston reported that Tim Todd beat Greg Elder in a re-run of the Associated Student Government presidential election, two days after the Herald had indexed the first contest as no contest and endorsed Elder. The same issue carried a letter from Shannon Ragland asking that ASG's name be cleared. The archive previously recorded that the published result of the 1987 race did not survive; this settles it.
src_label: Herald 62:54, 16 Apr 1987, "Tim Todd Beats Greg Elder in Election Re-Run"

title: Conflicts and walkouts close the year
body: Leigh Eagleston reported that conflicts and walkouts had finished off the Associated Student Government year. The same issue carried an editorial saying the organisation had image problems and should leave its antics behind, and a letter from Tommy Johnson encouraging its officers.
src_label: Herald 62:56, 23 Apr 1987, "Conflicts, Walkouts Finish Off Associated Student Government Year"

title: The Herald calls the congress paralyzed
body: Doug Gott wrote a piece headlined that Associated Student Government was paralyzed, in the last week of the spring term. It followed a fortnight of election re-run, walkouts and letters, and the surviving index preserves only the headline.

title: The filing deadline for congress seats is extended
body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government filing deadline had been extended. It was the first of the year's several notices about seats that had not attracted candidates.
src_label: Herald 63:6, 15 Sep 1987, "Associated Student Government Filing Deadline Extended"

title: A member loses his seat
body: The Herald reported that Associated Student Government member Nick Hicks had lost his seat. Five days later the body moved to get tough on absenteeism.
src_label: Herald 63:17, 22 Oct 1987, "Associated Student Government Member Loses Seat – Nick Hicks"

title: Eighty-one students ratify the amendments
body: Eighty-one students voted to approve the constitutional amendments that had gone before the body two days earlier. The same issue reported that the congress had voted to withdraw its support from the Kentucky Intercollegiate Student Legislature, a membership it had been debating since September.
src_label: Herald 63:23, 12 Nov 1987, "81 Students Vote to Approve Student Government Association Amendments"

title: An impeachment process is begun against a member
body: Jill Duff reported that the body had begun an impeachment process against congress member Bill Schilling. The surviving index preserves the headline and the reporter's name but not the article text, so the grounds of the complaint are not recorded here.
src_label: Herald 63:25, 19 Nov 1987, "Student Government Association Begins Bill Schilling Impeachment Process"

title: The impeachment request is dropped
body: Two weeks after beginning the process, the body dropped its request for impeachment. The same issue carried an editorial calling the episode a tragedy that should not mean curtains for the organisation, and a Julia Barry cartoon drawing its members as clowns. No source found records the vote by which the request was dropped.
src_label: Herald 63:27, 3 Dec 1987, "Student Government Association Drops Request for Impeachment"

title: A watchdog committee replaces the impeachment
body: Jill Duff reported that Bill Schilling was under the eye of a watchdog committee, the measure the body adopted in place of impeachment. The same issue carried letters from William Fogle explaining the organisation's actions and from Van C. Hodge Jr. saying the issue remained.
src_label: Herald 63:29, 10 Dec 1987, "Bill Schilling Under Eye of Watchdog Committee"

title: A class president quits mid-year
body: Dorren Klausnitzer reported that senior class president Greg Robertson had quit. It was the first of the vacancies the body would spend the spring explaining.
src_label: Herald 63:33, 21 Jan 1988, "Student Government Association Senior Class President Greg Robertson Quits"

title: Schilling asks for a leave of absence
body: Dorren Klausnitzer reported that Bill Schilling had asked the body for a leave of absence, eleven weeks after it dropped the impeachment request against him. The same issue carried an editorial telling the organisation it needed better ideas rather than gimmicks.
src_label: Herald 63:43, 25 Feb 1988, "Bill Schilling Asks for Leave of Absence"

title: An officer is reported arrested
body: The Herald reported the arrest of an Associated Student Government officer, printing the name as William Byron Shilling; earlier items in the same volume print the surname Schilling. The surviving index preserves only the headline: no charge is recorded, and no source found reports any outcome. The minutes of 1 March 1988 record that Schilling was running for the ASG presidency.
src_label: Herald 63:46, 17 Mar 1988, "Associated Student Government Officer Arrested"

title: Two of thirty-two congress positions contested
body: The Herald reported that only 2 of the 32 Associated Student Government positions on the spring ballot were contested. It is the only explicit seat count for Congress found in this period.
src_label: Herald 63:47, 22 Mar 1988, "2 of 32 Associated Student Government Positions Contested"

title: Congress tables a proposal against the university president
body: The body tabled a proposal directed against university president Kern Alexander. The same issue reported that the election was officially under way and that the congress would consider adding condom machines; Alexander announced his resignation nineteen days later.
src_label: Herald 63:48, 24 Mar 1988, "Associated Student Government Tables Proposal Against Kern Alexander"

title: The election appeal continues into the fall
body: Rebecca Fullen reported that Bruce Cambron was still appealing the spring presidential election, five months after the result. The same issue announced the freshman election for the following Tuesday.
src_label: Herald 64:9, 22 Sep 1988, "Bruce Cambron Still Appeals Election"

title: Congress changes its committees
body: Rebecca Fullen reported that the Associated Student Government had made committee changes. The same issue reported Dan Knowles winning the freshman election. The surviving index preserves only the headlines, so which committees changed is not recorded here.
src_label: Herald 64:15, 13 Oct 1988, "Associated Student Government Makes Committee Changes"

title: A congress seat goes to a run-off
body: Rebecca Fullen reported that Lori Easton had won an Associated Student Government run-off race. The same issue reported the new Wednesday afternoon hotline and the mock presidential election.
src_label: Herald 64:17, 20 Oct 1988, "Lori Easton Wins Associated Student Government Run Off Race"

title: Kevin Colon wins the freshman election
body: The Herald reported that Kevin Colon had won the Associated Student Government freshman election held on 15 October. Two weeks earlier the paper had reported turnout at the fall elections as low with results not yet ready.
src_label: Herald 67:15, 17 Oct 1991, "Kevin Colon Wins Freshman Election"

title: Minutes record a resignation
body: The minutes of the 21 January 1992 meeting record the resignation of Patrick McBrian, alongside the retreat, Who's Who of American College Students and health services.
src_label: TopSCHOLAR, SGA Records: Meeting Minutes, 21 Jan 1992

title: The student regent advisory committee bill fails after amendment
body: Nikita Stewart reported that the bill to create an advisory committee for the student regent failed in the Associated Student Government once it had been altered. Bill #92-01-S had been introduced on 28 January by Greg Butler, Mistianna Holcomb, Melony Jones and Melissa Maggard and sponsored by the Public Relations committee.
src_label: Herald 67:36, 6 Feb 1992, "Altered Bill Fails in Associated Student Government"

title: A bill would add three non-traditional seats
body: Nikita Stewart reported a bill that would add three non-traditional students to the Associated Student Government. The following issue carried a Patrick Richardson cartoon on non-traditional students at a meeting. No source found records whether the bill passed.
src_label: Herald 67:42, 27 Feb 1992, "Bill Would Add 3 Non-traditional Students to Associated Student Government"

title: Congress kills a bill of its own that was not being enforced
body: Nikita Stewart reported that the Associated Student Government had killed a bill that was not being enforced. The same issue reported candidates readying for the 14 April election.
src_label: Herald 67:47, 26 Mar 1992, "Associated Student Government Kills Bill That Wasn't Being Enforced"

title: Vacancies on the agenda in the last full spring meeting
body: The minutes of 24 March 1992 record vacancies among the business taken up, alongside a meeting with Wendell Ford's staff, the banquet, dormitory visitation, a call-a-thon and environmental issues.
src_label: TopSCHOLAR, SGA Records: Meeting Minutes, 24 Mar 1992

title: The renaming is introduced as a constitutional amendment
body: Bill #92-10-S, introduced 1 April 1992, was a bill to change Associated Student Government to Student Government Association. It is the instrument behind the vote the body took six days later.
src_label: SGA Legislation, Bill #92-10-S, "Constitutional Amendment to Rename ASG to SGA"

title: Students vote on the amendments
body: Jim Hannah reported that students were voting that day on the Associated Student Government amendments, on the same ballot as the presidential election. Two days later the Herald reported that about 1,200 students had turned out.
src_label: Herald 67:52, 14 Apr 1992, "Students Vote Today on Associated Student Government Amendments"

title: Congress voted two members into open seats
body: Under unfinished business on 12 October 1993, Congress voted on open positions and seated Stephanie McCarty as a sophomore representative and Lori Haycraft as a representative at large. The same minutes record Resolution 93-3-F tabled back to the Campus Improvements Committee and eight members absent at roll call.

title: A bylaws bill, and the bylaws suspended the same night
body: On 29 March 1994 Congress took first readings of Bill 94-4-S on the Points of Light programme, Bill 94-5-S amending the bylaws, Bill 94-6-S on an athletics calendar and Resolution 94-5-S on funding a social work faculty member. It then suspended the bylaws to consider Resolution 94-5-S, which was amended and passed that evening rather than waiting for a second reading.

title: Twenty-one seats stood open in Congress
body: At the meeting of 28 February 1995 the secretary read the open positions into the minutes: two senior off-campus, two junior off-campus, four non-traditional and one graduate college seat, plus one seat each in East, Florence Schneider, McLean, South, West, New Co-Ed, Sorority Hall, Bemis, Keen, Central and Barnes Campbell halls. Congress voted three people into seats that night, leaving eighteen unfilled.

title: Bill 96-2-S put constitutional amendments before Congress
body: Bill 96-2-S, Constitutional Amendments, is dated 20 February 1996, the same day as Resolution 96-2-S on a dead week. They are the only two numbered measures from the spring 1996 session that survive in either archive. The amendments went on the April 1996 student ballot.

title: Congress ordered its own legislation filed in the library
body: Resolution 99-2-S, Legislation to be Filed at Helm Library, is dated 16 February 1999. It is the only measure in the block that addresses where the branch's own record was to be kept.

title: Three constitutional amendment bills in one sitting
body: Bills 99-7-S, 99-8-S and 99-10-S, each amending the SGA constitution, are all dated 2 March 1999. The texts were not retrievable, so what they changed and whether they passed is not established here.

title: Congress legislated on its own membership
body: Bill 99-16-S, Congressional Eligibility Requirements, and Bill 99-17-S, Executive Office Hour Requirements, are both dated 30 March 1999. A week earlier Bill 99-14-S had revised the duties of the Coordinator of Committees, and on 23 February 1999 Bill 99-6-S had dealt with hall representative notices. Their texts were not retrievable.

title: A voided race re-run, and won by a wider margin
body: After the Judicial Council's ruling on the spring elections, the Herald of 27 April 1999 reported Ryan Morrison winning an SGA election. This repository's own research file .research/fillins-1985-2000.json records that the Council voided the vice president of finance race over election code violations by candidate Joe Matheis, and that Morrison beat Matheis 346-99 in the re-run on 26 April 1999.

title: Bill 03-10-F, New Constitution and Bylaws, entered the record
body: SGA's own legislation archive dates Bill 03-10-F, New Constitution and Bylaws, to 10 November 2003. Robert Watkins, chair of the Legislative Research Committee, wrote it. It was the vehicle by which the rewrite of the constitution reached Congress.
src_label: WKU SGA legislation archive, 2003, archived 17 Jan 2005

title: Congress passed the new constitution and bylaws by general consent
body: At the fourteenth meeting of the year, with 25 of 43 members present, Robert Watkins defended Bill 03-10-F by saying the old constitution had too many problems and that he had taken everyone's ideas into account in writing the new one. Members asked about the meaning of the word maniple, which the minutes note would be amended to malleable, and about the discrimination clause. There was a motion, a second and no debate, and the bill passed with general consent.

title: Judicial Council ruled the president had violated the constitution
body: The Judicial Council reported to Congress that it had been asked for three interpretations. It defined a complete semester of membership as one begun before the fourth Congress meeting, held that exemptions for executive candidacy turned on the individual case, and ruled that President John Bradley violated the constitution by making attendance mandatory at the plus/minus grading rally, since no member of one governmental body could order a member of another to act.

title: The rewrite reported: 75 seats to 35, Congress to Senate
body: The Herald reported that the proposed constitution would cut the elected legislative membership from 75 to 35 and rename Congress the Senate, with four representatives from each class, two graduate students and seventeen at-large members. Residence hall, academic college and off-campus seats would be eliminated, the vice presidency of finance folded into administration, public relations made a directorship, and a chief of staff, speaker of the senate and senate secretary created. Watkins said it was sometimes difficult to get proportional representation with the existing number of positions to fill, and Bradley said all 75 positions had never been filled during his time in SGA. No vote had yet been taken because two-thirds of the body had not been present at the past two meetings.
src_label: Herald, 22 Jan 2004, "Student government considering new constitution" (Wayback)

title: About 13 members struck from the Congress roll for absences
body: The Herald reported that within the two weeks before 12 February 2004 the Judicial Council removed about 13 Congress members who had missed more than three meetings from the roll, and that the members had also been called or emailed about their participation. Vice President of Administration Jessica Martin said some could not attend because of scheduling conflicts. The removals, with new members sworn in, brought the roll to 29 and allowed a two-thirds attendance. The day of the removals is not recorded in the sources found.
src_label: Herald, 12 Feb 2004, "SGA approves new constitution on fifth attempt" (Wayback)

title: Congress approved the constitution on the fifth attempt
body: Congress unanimously approved the new constitution and set of bylaws on Tuesday 10 February 2004, with 25 of 29 members present. The Herald reported it was the fifth attempt, the earlier ones having failed because the two-thirds of members needed to vote on the legislation were not present. Watkins called it disturbing that it took so long to get two-thirds of Congress to the meetings and said it reiterated the need for a new system; Bradley said a smaller Congress would help remedy attendance.
src_label: Herald, 12 Feb 2004, "SGA approves new constitution on fifth attempt" (Wayback)

title: Bill 04-2-S, Congress Attendance Motivator
body: SGA's legislation archive lists Bill 04-2-S, titled Congress Attendance Motivator, dated 25 February 2004. The text of the bill has not been located.
src_label: WKU SGA legislation archive, 2004, archived 17 Jan 2005

title: A student commentary attacked the at-large majority
body: On the day of the referendum the Herald printed a commentary arguing that 17 of the new senate's 35 seats would be at-large and so not accountable to any specific constituency, that vacancies after the fall elections could still be filled by appointment, and that graduate seats would convert to at-large seats if unfilled. It urged students to demand the at-large places be converted to class representatives.
src_label: Herald, 9 Mar 2004, "New constitution should promote better representation of student body" (Wayback)

title: Students ratified the new constitution 116 to 16
body: Students approved the proposed constitution and bylaws in an online referendum held on TopNet on Tuesday 9 March 2004. Bradley reported 116 votes in favour, 16 against and no abstentions, out of 132 cast; about 18,000 students had been enrolled the previous semester. Watkins said the old system of electing 75 legislative seats had been idealistic; Associate Justice Dana Lockhart said the same dangers were still present because open seats could still be filled by appointment.

title: Proposed constitution stalls for want of two-thirds of the body
body: The Herald reported that the proposed constitution had not had its second reading because two-thirds of the SGA body had not been present at either of the past two meetings. Robert Watkins, chair of the legislative research committee and author of the document, said it would cut elected legislative seats from 75 to 35 and rename Congress the senate, with four representatives from each class year, two graduate students and 17 at large. President John Bradley said all 75 positions had never been filled during his time in SGA.

title: Congress approves the new constitution on the fifth attempt
body: The Herald of 12 February 2004 reported that the Student Government Association had approved the new constitution on its fifth attempt. The index of that issue is the only text of the report this archive holds; the full article has not been read.

title: Nine students file for 28 spring senate seats
body: Nine students filed to run for the senate seats on the 16 and 17 March ballot, against the 28 of the 35 seats the proposed constitution assigned to a spring election. President John Bradley said the judicial council would decide the following year how to fill positions with no candidates. The nine were Melissa Paris, Katharine Pettit, Brittany Fausey, John Law, Alicia Bachicha, Abby Lovan, Sarah Cecil, Mason Stevenson and Robert Watkins.

title: Students ratify the constitution 116 to 16
body: The constitution and bylaws were ratified in an online referendum that closed at midnight on 9 March 2004, by 116 votes to 16 with no abstentions, out of roughly 18,000 students enrolled the previous semester. The Herald reported that the documents cut the legislative branch from 75 seats to 35, abolished the vice presidencies of finance and public relations, and created the offices of speaker of the senate, secretary of the senate, chief of staff and director of academic and student affairs. Associate Justice Dana Lockhart warned that open legislative seats could still be filled by appointment rather than election.

title: Senators move to ask the Judicial Council to censure the president
body: The Herald of 7 March 2006 reported that SGA senators would ask for a judicial censure of President Katie Dawson, and the issue of 9 March reported that the senators had delayed the decision. Under the bylaws then in force, a censure request signed by no fewer than ten people obliged the Judicial Council to investigate and to issue a censure if it found the officer neglecting their duties. The archive holds only the index entries for these two reports; whether a censure was ever issued is not established in any source found.
src_label: College Heights Herald 81:34, 7 Mar 2006 and 81:35, 9 Mar 2006, indexes (TopSCHOLAR)

title: South Campus asks for a voice in the senate
body: The Herald reported that students and faculty at South Campus wanted a student government there and wanted it attached to SGA. Senator VaShae Swope planned an interest table at South Campus that day to collect comment cards. Associate professor Quentin Hollis said it had been about five years since South Campus had a student government; associate professor Michelle Hollis said the aim was a group of about ten students to attend main campus SGA meetings, and that she had met former SGA President Johnathon Boles about it before he resigned. The constitution in force reserved no senate seat for South Campus.

title: Senate approves a $109,040.66 operating budget
body: At the second meeting of the eighth senate, with 19 of 23 senators present, the senate voted to approve the 2009-10 operating budget of $109,040.66, with three abstentions. Organizational aid was capped at $40,000, Provide-A-Ride and non-emergency medical transport at $15,000, and $20,000 was left for the senate to spend as it saw fit. The same meeting confirmed the president's cabinet nominations, including his brother as chief of staff with two abstentions, and a former executive vice president told the senate from the floor that he questioned its integrity for approving that appointment.

title: A fourth senator resigns a week after the publications committee walkout
body: Senator Skylar Jordan came before the senate on 27 October 2009 and submitted his resignation, a week after Michel Stephens, Emmett Stephens and Daniel Shaw had resigned at the meeting of 20 October. The roll stood at 30 senators that night, down from 32. The Judicial Council reported it had made four decisions, two of them concerning the resignations of senators and one on attendance.

title: Senate elects next year's Speaker
body: The senate elected Austin Wingate speaker of the Student Senate at its meeting of 13 April 2010, the spring election of a Speaker for the following academic year that the constitution as amended in 2005 required. The Judicial Council reported at the same meeting that it had approved the spring election results and was bringing three senators up for judicial review.

title: Executive Cabinet vetoed the dance marathon funding bill
body: Bill 2-11-F, funding for the WKU Danceathon "RAGE," was first read on 4 October 2011 and passed the Senate on 11 October. SGA's own legislation archive records the outcome at the executive stage as "Vetoed," the only veto listed for that session. The archive records no override vote.
src_label: WKU SGA Legislation Archive, Fall 2011 - Spring 2012 table

title: Judicial Council amendment passed on its second reading after being voided
body: Resolution 1-14-S was first read on 4 February 2014 and declared invalid by the Executive Council later that month because too few senators had been present for the vote. The legislation archive records its second reading on 25 March 2014, and the constitution as later published carries the changes: seven justices, a Chief Justice chosen by a majority of the Council, and an Associate Chief Justice.
src_label: SGA Resolution 1-14-S; WKU SGA Legislation Archive

title: Senate adopted amendments to the Glasgow campus constitution
body: Resolution 6-14-F was first read on 28 October 2014 and passed on 11 November. It stated that the Glasgow Student Body, incorporated as a regional affiliate two years earlier, had been unable to raise enough student interest to fill and maintain an executive cabinet, student senate and judicial council. Seth Church wrote it, with GSBA president Samantha Johnson listed as a contact.

title: Bylaw amendment required roll-call voting and posted minutes
body: Resolution 3-15-S, first read 24 February 2015 and passed 3 March, added Bylaw 2.7 requiring every vote in any branch to be taken by roll call or electronic voting, recorded in the minutes, and posted by the Director of Information Technology or the Secretary of the Senate within one week. The text set the amendment to take effect on 17 March 2015. Zach Jones and Seth Church wrote it.
src_label: SGA Resolution 3-15-S, Resolution to Adopt an Amendment to the Bylaws to Increase Accountability

title: Senate recognised the Elizabethtown/Ft. Knox Student Body Association
body: Resolution 1-15-F, written by President Jay Todd Richey, was first read on 1 September 2015 and passed on 8 September. It recognised the Elizabethtown/Ft. Knox Student Body Association, which had asked to become a regional affiliate and to gain representation within SGA by elected representatives from its campus.

title: Four senate seats reported open at the fourth meeting
body: At the fourth meeting of the Fourteenth Senate, President Jay Todd Richey told senators that four senate seats were open and asked them to recruit. He reported at the same meeting that he had met the chancellors of the regional campuses about a listening tour. The Judicial Council reminded senators that more than three unexcused absences brought judicial review.

title: Senate set a deadline for new business
body: Resolution 3-15-F, first read 29 September 2015 and passed 6 October, amended Rule XXVII of the Rules of the Senate to require any bill or resolution to reach the Speaker of the Senate and the Legislative Research chair by 5 p.m. on the Monday before a regular meeting, or two days before a specially called meeting, to appear under new business. Emily Anne Pride and Megan Skaggs wrote it.
src_label: SGA Resolution 3-15-F, Resolution to Adopt a Senate-Wide "New Business" Policy

title: A grade point average amendment failed in the Senate
body: The Herald of 9 February 2016 carried Dustin Skipworth's report, indexed as "Grade Point Average Amendment Fails in Student Government Association." The 2.5 cumulative requirement stayed in the constitution until April 2017.
src_label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 91, No. 5, 9 Feb 2016, WKU Archives index

title: Art and physics funding bills passed a second time after the judicial ruling
body: SGA's legislation archive lists the bills to assist the art and physics departments twice: passed on 10 November 2015 under the numbers R09-15-F and R08-15-F, and passed again on 16 February 2016 under the numbers B09-15-F and B08-15-F. The Judicial Council had ruled the earlier versions unconstitutional on 3 December 2015 under the bylaw restricting SGA funding to students.
src_label: WKU SGA Legislation Archive, Fall 2015 - Spring 2016 table; Herald, 3 Dec 2015

title: Judicial Council found the veto of Resolution 1-17-S constitutional
body: Chief Justice Cody Cox reported to the Senate at its eighteenth meeting that the Executive Board's veto of Resolution 1-17-S had been found constitutional. He used the same report to remind senators to file Senate excuse forms for missed meetings.

title: Senate refused to strip the executive of the power to propose legislation
body: Bill 26-17-S, written by senator-at-large William Hurst and sponsored by the Public Relations Committee, would have struck "Make proposals on matters of policy" from Constitution 2.10.1.2, ending the executive branch's power to propose legislation. It was first and second read on 4 April 2017 and failed 7-22-1.

title: Senate required biweekly reports of executive discretionary spending
body: Bill 24-17-S amended Constitution 2.5.3 to add biweekly reports of executive discretionary spending to the Administrative Vice President's duties, arguing that senate discretionary spending was set out in legislation while executive discretionary spending was not as easily accessible. It was first and second read on 4 April 2017 and passed 29-0-1. Students ratified it in the April referendum.

title: Academic Affairs and Student Affairs merged into one committee
body: Bill 28-17-S, first read 18 April 2017 and passed 28-0-0 on 25 April, combined the two committees into the Academic and Student Affairs Committee. Its text said the Student Affairs Committee's duty to address cultural issues had passed to the MyCampusToo committee and that the two committees overlapped heavily on scholarship work. The chairs of both committees were among the authors.

title: Bill 12-21-S moved most Senate seats into the spring election
body: Bill 12-21-S, authored by Tess Welch, Dawson McCoun and Garrett Edmonds, had its first reading on 2 March 2021. It removed the academic-college senators, the international senator and three at-large seats from the fall ballot, leaving only three freshman, one graduate and one Gatton Academy seat to the autumn, and corrected a clause that still described two graduate senators. The bill argued that thirteen seats, nearly a third of the Senate, had been arriving too late to vote on the annual budget.

title: A constitutional amendment passed 31-0 and was vetoed the same day
body: Bill 13-22-S, written by Emily Bunning and Alex Cissell of the Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee to restate that committee's duties, had its second reading on 22 February 2022. The face of the document records an initial Senate vote of 31 in favour and none against, and a veto on 22 February 2022. A replacement, Bill 22-22-S, was first read on 8 March and passed both the Senate and the Executive Cabinet.

title: The seventh standing committee is created
body: Bill 21-22-S, first read 8 March and second read 22 March 2022, amended the constitution to establish a Community Relations Committee to advocate for students' needs in Bowling Green, encourage volunteer service and coordinate yearly voter drives. Its authors were Margaret Glaser, Emily Bunning and Cole Bornefeld, sponsored by the Outreach and Student Experience and Legislative Operations committees. The committee completed the seven-committee structure that the constitution still carries.

title: Pride sponsorship passed the Senate and was not passed by the Executive Cabinet
body: Bill 2-22-F, by Senator Meghan Pierce, allocated $250 to sponsor Bowling Green Pride and was read twice on 27 September 2022. SGA's own legislative archive records the bill as passed by the Senate and not passed by the Executive Cabinet. Herald coverage of the meeting reported the Senate vote and did not report the cabinet's action.
src_label: WKU SGA Legislation Archive, Fall 2022 - Spring 2023

title: Senate renamed three of its committees 36-1
body: Bill 4-22-F, authored by Speaker Julie Mishchuk and Senator Caleb Collins, was read on 4 and 11 October 2022 and carried 36 votes to 1. It cited a lack of clarity in the naming of constitutional committees and struck the abbreviations, making the Committee of Enrollment and Student Experience the Enrollment and Student Experience Committee, the Committee of Outreach and Student Experience the Outreach and Student Engagement Committee, and the Committee for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Committee.

title: The committee merger passed the Senate but not the Executive Cabinet
body: Bill 44-23-S, by Speaker Julie Mishchuk with committee chairs Sydney Denney and Matt Gadd, would have merged the Community Relations and the Outreach and Student Engagement committees into a single Community Relations and Outreach Committee. It was read on 11 and 18 April 2023. SGA's legislative archive records it as passed by the Senate and not passed by the Executive Cabinet, and the constitutions posted for 2023-24 and afterwards continue to list the two committees separately.
src_label: SGA Bill 44-23-S and WKU SGA Legislation Archive

title: Fourteen constitutional amendments were read together
body: On 12 March 2024 the Senate gave a first reading to bills 19-24-S through 32-24-S, a single package drafted by a constitutional referendum committee and sponsored by the Legislative Operations Committee and the Judicial Council. The package abolished the directorships of information technology and enrollment and student experience, renamed the Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President as Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, raised the grade point average floors to 2.75 and 2.5, required removal after a second censure in a year, required documented executive spending, obliged the Legislative Operations Committee to ensure bills are nonpartisan, and moved committee-head appointments to the Speaker. The second reading was held on 28 March 2024.

title: The DEI committee amendment went to the ballot without a settled number
body: The bill renaming the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee the Action and Opportunity Committee was read twice on 3 April 2025. It also redistributed the committee's members across the other committees except Legislative Operations, and replaced the reference to Chief Diversity Officers, a title WKU no longer used. The document itself is headed "Bill X-24-S" with no number filled in; SGA's legislative archive lists it as Bill 22-25-S, and Herald coverage called it Bill 21-25-S. Students ratified it in the 13-15 April election with 88 percent in favour.
src_label: SGA constitutional amendment on the DEI Committee, filed as bill_21_25_s

title: A campus safety committee appears outside the constitution's seven
body: Resolution 1-26-S, read on 3 and 10 February 2026, designated 30 March to 3 April 2026 as WKU Campus Safety and Security Week in response to violence at other universities. It was sponsored by a Campus Safety and Security Committee alongside the Legislative Operations Committee. That committee is not one of the seven named in the constitution; the Senate minutes of 14 April 2026 record its work reported jointly with the Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee under chair Veronica Butler.

title: Students ratify a constitution that strengthens the judicial system
body: The student body approved a new Associated Students constitution by 1,397 votes to 697, with 2,094 students voting, about 23 per cent of those eligible. The Herald reported that key issues in the document were a student bill of rights and strengthening the judicial system, and that it would go next to the University administration and ultimately to the Board of Regents. The Rules and Election Committee, which usually handled campus elections, had refused to supervise the referendum, saying its members were too involved in end of semester activities; a committee headed by Ashabraner ran it instead.

title: Congress passes the revised constitution 23 to 0
body: Associated Students voted 23 to 0 to accept the proposed constitution; twenty-two votes in favour were needed for passage, and several members had left the meeting early, so a nearly unanimous vote was required. The Herald said the vote culminated nearly a year and a half of deliberations by the administration and the Associated Students, and set out the schedule: the administration to receive the document on 3 March and approve or question any part by 10 March, then a referendum.

title: Referendum ratifies the constitution that revised the judicial branch
body: Students approved the revised constitution 157 to 16 in a two-day referendum on 29 and 30 March 1972; fewer than two per cent of Western's 10,133 students voted, and a simple majority was required. The Herald reported that the judicial branch of the constitution had been revised to clarify the judicial processes on campus. The same revision created a second vice-presidency, remade representation on Congress and changed the organisation's name to Associated Student Government. It became effective immediately following the installation of new officers, scheduled for 27 April 1972.

title: Judicial Council rules Kim Weaver ineligible for president
body: The Rules and Elections Committee ruled presidential candidate Kim Weaver ineligible on 4 April under Article 2, Section 2, Part A-4 of the newly ratified ASG constitution, which required candidates to be resident students carrying a minimum of six hours while in office; Weaver was a legislative intern in Frankfort that semester. The committee reversed itself at 4 p.m. on 5 April after a closed hearing that Weaver's attorney was allowed to attend. The Judicial Council, which the Herald described as five members appointed by president Linda Jones or former president John Lyne, met at 7 p.m. the same evening on the other candidates' appeal and ruled Weaver ineligible. The council said it did not recognise the University's definition of a resident student and defined 'in attendance' as physically attending classes on the Western campus.

title: Student Affairs Board overrules the Judicial Council and reinstates Weaver
body: The nine-member Student Affairs Board heard three and a half hours of testimony, deliberated for one and a half hours in executive session, and reinstated Kim Weaver as a candidate. Weaver's petition rested on five points, the first that he was not afforded a fair and impartial hearing before the Judicial Council; the others were that the council lacked jurisdiction, excluded relevant testimony, gave inadequate notice, and decided against the weight of the evidence. Dean Charles Keown, who presided, said the board upheld Weaver's petition and overruled the Judicial Council on point one. Judicial Council chairman John Knight sat on the board and refused to disqualify himself, so Carter presented the council's view of the case.

title: Five of eight members disqualify themselves and the council declines Hatfield's appeal
body: The Judicial Council declined to hear an appeal by Bob Hatfield, who had been eliminated in the ASG presidential primary, against a Rules and Elections Committee decision. Five of the eight members of the council disqualified themselves in a statement issued at a pre-hearing conference. Hatfield had contended that Kim Weaver's campaign spending breached the committee's regulations, which capped spending at $150 for the primary or $175 including the general election, with donations of funds and materials counted in. The committee, meeting in special session late on 12 April, had ruled that Weaver's expenditures did not violate its guidelines and overruled his protest.

title: Hall hearing boards die
body: The Herald reported under the headline 'Hall Hearing Boards Die a Natural Death' that the residence hall hearing board system had ended. Those boards had been the source of the disciplinary appeals that ran to the Associated Students Judicial Council from 1971-72. The archive does not yet hold the text of this article; the digitised issue carries no machine-readable layer.

title: Congress opens impeachment proceedings against the Judicial Council chairman
body: Six congressmen moved to impeach Gerard Faulk, chairman of the ASG Judicial Council, charging incompetence. Six of the 43 congress members present voted to endorse impeachment; the constitution required at least five members to initiate the action. Charles Keown, dean of student affairs, said it was the first time impeachment proceedings had been introduced in congress in ASG history. Marc Levy, who made the motion, cited Faulk's handling of congressman Tom Blair's allegations against President Steve Henry, which congress had sent to the council on 2 March and which the council never met to discuss, and the fund misuse case against treasurer David Payne. Faulk called the move a political manoeuvre and said he would fight it. Three Judicial Council members contacted by the Herald the next day were unaware the proceedings had begun.

title: An organization chart names the judicial branch for 1976-77
body: An ASG organization chart for 1976-77 sets out three branches and lists the Judicial Branch as Gerard Faulk, chairman, with Charlotte Antoine, Joe Phillips, Ed Mitchell, Nancy Holman, Patricia Cook and Megan Lake, and three alternates, Teri Sell, Sue Ellen Young and Jim Matthews. The same chart lists the executive officers elected in April 1976 and records the congress dismissals, resignations and appointments of the session. TopSCHOLAR dates the chart to 1 August 1976.
src_label: WKU SGA Records, SGA Organization Chart, 1976-77

title: The new Judicial Council is itself disputed
body: A week after the council was sworn in, the Herald reported a dispute over whether ASG president David Payne had the authority to appoint it and whether appointing his roommate, Bowling Green sophomore Bob Dillard, was a conflict of interest. Payne said he understood he was going against the constitution, which required appointments no later than two weeks after the start of the fall term, because Marcel Bush had not appointed the council in the autumn, and that ASG was working from an out-of-date constitution. Ragan said she had not known Dillard was Payne's roommate and that a conflict would have arisen only had he been made chairman; an unnamed member said the arrangement defeated the purpose of having a council at all. Bush said Payne had the power to appoint whom he chose but should have used better discretion. Adviser Ron Beck said he could see why some would object but did not think it would create a problem.
src_label: Herald 57:37, 4 Feb 1982, Kevin A. Francke, "Judicial appointments criticized"

title: A replaced council member writes to the Herald
body: Paul J. Deom, a senior, wrote that he was no longer on the Judicial Council because of the organisation's disregard for its own constitution. He said Steve Fuller had appointed him in autumn 1980 on the understanding that he would serve a three-year term under article IX, section 1, subsection B of the constitution then in force, and that the executive council and president had decided to replace him. He also disputed the statement that a new council was appointed each January, pointing to the constitutional rule that members take office no later than two weeks after the fall term begins.
src_label: Herald 57:37, 4 Feb 1982, letters page, Paul J. Deom, "Former Judicial Council member irked"

title: A complaint to disqualify Margaret Ragan is rejected
body: Glenn Sargent filed a complaint against Margaret Ragan saying she had not filed campaign expenditure forms 48 hours before the general election as the rules required. Five of the seven rules and elections committee members met with Canafax, Sargent and Ragan for two hours, deliberated for a further hour and decided Ragan would not be disqualified; Canafax said eight other candidates had also broken the rule and the committee did not think it grounds for disqualification. Sargent said he did not understand why the committee made rules it would not enforce; Ragan said missing the deadline was an oversight. The committee also raised the campaign spending limit from $200 to $300.

title: The 1986-87 Judicial Council roster
body: The surviving roster of the Associated Student Government Judicial Council for 1986-87 names seven regular members and three alternates, the establishment the constitution required. The regular members were Kent Groemling, Bill Schilling, Naheed Shafi, Jerry Castleberry, Dwight Auslion, Jennifer Borsch and Dan Woolen, who is marked as chair; the alternates were Stacey Crain, Keith Wallace and Mary Kate Erwin. TopSCHOLAR dates the roster to the 1986-87 school year, from August 1986 to May 1987.

title: Impeachment proceedings are begun against the administrative vice president
body: Eight Congress members signed a letter opening impeachment proceedings against Bill Schilling, ASG's administrative vice president, on Tuesday 17 November 1987. The letter charged that he had illegally altered the amended constitution, misused student government funds, failed to fulfil his responsibilities, presented a negative image of student government and was not in good standing with the university. President Tim Todd called the alterations serious and said they had deleted a clause requiring officers to be in good standing and had raised the number of Congress signatures needed to start an impeachment from five to eight. Schilling said no clauses were purposely deleted and that if a clause was missing it had been left out inadvertently; Brandenburg sophomore Beth Rountree said she had typed the amended constitution at his request and that any changes were her fault. Schilling said he was not in good standing because a woman had been in his Poland Hall room ten minutes after visitation ended; Dave Parrott, director of Residence Life, said visitation violations were too minor to put anyone on disciplinary probation. Schilling had resigned on 26 October as administrative vice president of the Residence Hall Association after that body refused him a leave of absence, and its Rules and Elections Committee had found him no longer eligible to hold office there.
src_label: Herald 63:25, 19 Nov 1987, Jill Duff, "ASG begins Schilling impeachment process"

title: A watchdog agreement replaces the impeachment trial
body: On Monday 30 November 1987, the night before Congress was to sit as a judicial body and vote on removing him, Schilling signed an agreement with four of the eight members who had requested proceedings. Under it a committee had to approve his conduct in representing student government, his spending of its funds and his requests for typing by its secretary, and monitored the content of his interviews with the media and his memos to anyone outside the organisation. Hollie Hale, Kevin Hargrave, Kristina Hayden, Elaine Burge, Anne Zoellner and Schilling signed. Hale said that if he broke the agreement the signatories would start proceedings again, and called it basically a watchdog. The agreement was to run through the following semester.
src_label: Herald 63:29, 10 Dec 1987, Jill Duff, "Schilling under eye of 'watchdog' committee"

title: The impeachment request is rescinded and no vote is taken
body: At a six-minute meeting on Tuesday 1 December 1987, fourteen days after the proceedings began, secretary Danielle Williamson read a letter from Greg Robertson, Hollie Hale, Elaine Burge, Kevin Hargrave and Kristina Hayden withdrawing their motion and citing new evidence. With five of the eight names removed, the request fell short and no vote was taken on removing Schilling. Van Hodge, Becky Hack and Robin Kinman wanted to continue. Hargrave and Hodge later wrote that the group had not followed Robert's Rules of Order, student government's parliamentary authority, in starting the proceedings. Bill Fogle, a Western graduate and former Congress member acting as Schilling's counsel and not a lawyer, had met signatories the day before; Lynn Groemling, chairwoman of the Legislative Research Committee, said they were told they could be sued if they did not withdraw, and dean of Student Life Howard Bailey said students had told him they were threatened with lawsuits. Fogle said the threat of a lawsuit was never used to swing anyone's vote. Schilling apologised to Congress, said he was relieved, and remained in office. Assistant public safety director Horace Johnson said altering a university document could fall under third-degree forgery, a misdemeanour. No source found records any charge being brought.
src_label: Herald 63:27, 3 Dec 1987, Jill Duff, "ASG drops request for impeachment" and "Fogle threatened accusers with suit"

title: Nine Congress seats stand empty at the last meeting of the semester
body: Secretary Danielle Williamson reported that nine Congress positions were still open, five of them Academic Council seats: senior class vice president, the College of Business Administration representative and alternate, the Potter College alternate, the Ogden College representative and alternate, an on-campus representative and two off-campus representatives. Two seats were filled the same night, Chris Bilvis as an off-campus representative and Judith Williams as Graduate College alternate. Congress discussed the Schilling impeachment but voted to end the discussion until he could be present.

title: The Herald reported SGA bending its own election rules
body: A week before the spring election the Herald ran a report headlined that the Student Government Association was bending election rules. The digitised collection holds the issue as an index of headlines and bylines only, so the archive records the charge and not its substance.

title: The Judicial Council questioned Joe Matheis
body: Two days before the general election the Herald reported the Judicial Council questioning candidate Joe Matheis. It is the only item in the digitised Herald index between 1988 and 2005 whose headline names the Judicial Council.

title: SGA adopted rewritten election codes
body: The election codes carried the date 7 March 2000. They restated that the Judicial Council supervised all elections under Article IV, Section 5 of the constitution, and set spending limits of $750 for a president and vice president ticket, $400 for other executive candidates and $50 for a Congress seat, with a $100 cap on any one donor. They fixed the polling places, the 72-hour retention of ballots, the 48-hour window for recount requests, and the council's power to order a new election on a majority finding of impropriety. The Herald had reported in February and March 2000 that SGA was rewriting the codes to close loopholes and set spending limits.
src_label: WKU SGA, 2000 Election Codes as of 7 Mar 2000 (archived 2 Sep 2000)

title: Election violations confirmed after the spring 2002 election
