body: Twelve days after Jamie Sears won the presidency, the Herald reported under the headline "Election Violations Confirmed" on the Student Government Association. The digitised collection holds this issue as an index of headlines and bylines, and wkuherald.com's full text does not reach back to spring 2002, so the archive records that violations were confirmed and not which candidate, which rule or what the Judicial Council did about it.

title: The Judicial Council opened the year and adopted a code of conduct
body: The council met at 5 p.m. on 8 September 2003 with Chief Justice Troy Ransdell and Justices Gretchen Light and Joshua Collins present; a fifth justice had not been appointed. It discussed its code of conduct, elected Ransdell as its delegate to speak to Congress and Light as secretary, agreed a tentative standing meeting time of Mondays at 5 p.m. in the SGA office, and decided the election codes would be handled the following semester unless something forced them earlier. It adjourned at 6.15.
src_label: WKU SGA, Judicial Council minutes, 8 Sep 2003 (Wayback capture)

title: Three Congress members removed after attendance hearings
body: The Judicial Council met at 5.10 p.m. on 6 October 2003 with Chief Justice Troy Ransdell and Justices Scott Broadbent and Joshua Collins present. It conducted attendance hearings for Sara Hartley, Megan Gibson and Brandy Garrett, none of whom came to defend themselves, and removed all three for their absences. The meeting adjourned at 5.45.
src_label: WKU SGA, Judicial Council minutes, 6 Oct 2003 (Wayback capture)

title: The Judicial Council adopted the 2004 election codes
body: The 2004 Election Codes were adopted on 22 January 2004. They set filing between 1 February and 2 March, a candidates' orientation meeting at 7 p.m. on 17 February, spending limits of $450 for president, $400 for executive vice president, $350 for other Executive Cabinet offices and $50 for legislative candidates, and a three-business-day window for appeals. They also wrote the first online voting procedure into the codes, with polling on TopNet from 16 to 17 March 2004 and immediate disqualification for any candidate soliciting a voter's social security or identification number.
src_label: WKU SGA, 2004 Election Codes, adopted 22 Jan 2004 (archived 7 Sep 2004)

title: Judicial removals gave Congress the quorum to pass a new constitution
body: SGA congress unanimously approved a new constitution and bylaws on 10 February 2004 at its fifth attempt; the four earlier attempts had failed because two-thirds of Congress members were not present. Vice president of administration Jessica Martin said about thirteen Congress members who had missed more than three meetings had been removed from the roll by the Judicial Council within the previous two weeks, and that 25 of 29 members were present at the meeting that passed it. The constitution allowed 75 seats at the time.

title: Students ratified the new constitution, 116 to 16
body: The proposed constitution and bylaws went to a student referendum conducted on TopNet on 9 March 2004, from 12:01 a.m. to 11:59 p.m., with the timing announced by Chief Justice Troy Ransdell. It passed with 116 votes in favour and 16 against, no abstentions, out of 132 votes cast; about 18,000 students had been enrolled the previous semester. The changes cut the legislative branch from 75 seats to 35, required senators to be elected, abolished the vice presidencies of finance and public relations, and created a speaker of the senate, a secretary of the senate, a chief of staff and a director of academic and student affairs.

title: Nine candidates filed for 28 elected senate seats
body: Nine students filed to run for the legislative seats to be elected on 16 and 17 March 2004, out of 28 of the new senate's 35 seats due to be filled in the spring. President John Bradley said the Judicial Council would decide the following year how to fill the positions with no candidates. One student who filed late sought an exemption from the council to run, and Chief Justice Troy Ransdell said no exemptions would be granted after that Thursday because Information Technology needed time to add names to TopNet.

title: Election codes adopted, naming the Judicial Council supervisor of all SGA elections
body: The 2004 Election Codes were adopted on 22 January 2004 and opened by stating that the Judicial Council supervised all elections under the constitution's judicial article. They set a compulsory candidate orientation for 17 February, spending limits of $450 for president down to $50 for legislative candidates, itemised expenditure reports filed with the council in DUC 130, and a three-business-day window for appeals and protests after results. The calendar in the codes listed 9 March 1994 [sic: 2004] as the tentative date for the vote on the new constitution and 16-17 March for the elections.

title: Senators moved to ask for a judicial censure of the president
body: The College Heights Herald of 7 March 2006 carried an article by Katie Brandenburg indexed as senators asking for a judicial censure, naming SGA president Katie Dawson. The week before, the same reporter had covered executive vice president Mason Stevenson telling the Herald that SGA had problems. Under the bylaws a censure request signed by ten students obliged the Judicial Council to investigate.

title: Senators delayed the censure decision
body: The Herald of 9 March 2006 carried a follow-up by Katie Brandenburg indexed as senators delaying the censure decision. The archive holds only the index line for both articles; the full text was not reachable in this pass.

title: A complaint was filed against a party in the spring election
body: The Herald of 8 April 2008 carried an article by Neil Siders indexed as Skylar Jordan filing a complaint against the Red Towel Party, the slate whose presidential candidate had run against the sitting executive vice president. The election codes of this period sent appeals, protests and disqualifications to the Judicial Council, but the surviving index line does not say who heard the complaint or how it ended.

title: Council told the senate it was still working out office hours and attendance
body: At the eighth meeting of the eighth senate, held with 24 of 32 senators present, the Judicial Council reported it had met the previous week, had questions about office hours and planned an official decision the following week, and was still working on how to handle attendance. Three senators submitted resignations at the same meeting.

title: Chief Justice reported four Judicial Council decisions
body: With 19 of 30 senators present, the chief justice reported that the council had made four decisions: one on office hours, two on the resignation of senators, and one on attendance. He also told senators to bring him any complaints about technology on campus.

title: Senate suspended its bylaws to seat an associate justice
body: At the nineteenth meeting of the eighth senate, held with 21 of 30 senators present, the senate approved four presidential appointments as student senators and then moved Artilla Scisney from appointments to approvals by suspending the bylaws, approving her unanimously as associate justice. The SGA website listed her on the council by late May 2010.

title: Senate suspended its bylaws to approve the spring election codes the same night
body: The Judicial Council reported it had been working on the elections and that the previous day had been the deadline for finalising the ballot, and put the election codes before the senate. The senate suspended its bylaws to vote the same night, and the codes passed unanimously with no debate. The minutes file is dated 23 March 2010 although its header repeats the previous week's date.

title: Council certified the election results and referred three senators for review
body: Reporting to the senate on 13 April 2010, the Judicial Council said it had met and approved the election results, and that it was bringing three senators up for judicial review. The senate elected a new speaker at the same meeting.

title: Judicial Council issued three written opinions, each carried 5-0
body: On 28 August 2012 Chief Justice Chris Jankowski published three opinions, each recording a unanimous 5-0 vote of the council. One set out the judicial review procedure, one interpreted the attendance policy and defined excused and unexcused absences, and one ruled on two surplus at-large senators, letting them serve out their terms while barring the president from refilling those two seats until the constitutional composition was met.

title: SGA began publishing Judicial Council opinions online
body: A judicial opinions page appeared on SGA's website, last modified 5 September 2012, listing the three opinions of 28 August and stating that online publication of Judicial Council opinions was a new accountability initiative of the Dodds administration, with opinions to be uploaded as they became available. The page named Chief Justice Christopher Jankowski as the contact.

title: Judicial Council reviewed and approved the constitutional package before the senate voted
body: Resolution 5-13-S, first read on 19 February 2013 and read a second time on 26 February, records in its whereas clauses that the proposed amendments had been reviewed and approved by the Judicial Council under clause 4.5.9 of the constitution. Chief Justice Seth Church is listed among the resolution's contacts. The resolution referred the amendments to the student body for ratification on the spring 2013 ballot.

title: Council created an Election Code Advisory Board
body: In Opinion 2013FA-005 the Judicial Council established an Election Code Advisory Board under section 4.5.8 of the constitution, to rewrite election codes it described as having proven inadequate. The board was chaired by the chief justice, open to any SGA member or student willing to serve, and required to report to the Senate monthly until dissolved by a majority vote of the council. Its recommendations were not binding on the council.

title: Council overruled its own year-old joint campaigning rule
body: In Opinion 2014SP-001, In re joint campaigning (II), the Judicial Council overruled its 2013 opinion on candidates campaigning together and set a new formula: the lowest expenditure cap among joint campaigners, divided by their number, was the most each could put into shared material, and each then subtracted the whole joint total from their own allowance. The opinion worked the arithmetic for a senator pair and for a three-way presidential ticket, and said the council would take good-faith compliance leniently because the rule was new.

title: Council ruled abstentions count toward quorum
body: In Opinion 2014SP-002 the Judicial Council was asked whether Resolution 5-14-S had passed properly. It held that abstaining members cast neither a yes nor a no vote but concur with the majority of those voting, citing a 1988 Kentucky Attorney General opinion, and that abstaining members do count toward quorum because quorum refers to the number present. Since no senator had noted a lack of quorum, quorum was presumed throughout and the resolution passed. Chief Justice Seth Church delivered the opinion, joined by Julia Payne and Jackie Stewart; Megan Lemmons took no part.

title: All seven justices censured a senator on a ten-student petition
body: At a second emergency meeting the council took up a censure request signed by ten students, both senators and other WKU students, over Senator William Hurst's profanity, gestures and walking out of the previous emergency meeting. Chief Justice Annalicia Carlson refused Hurst's request for the petitioners' names and referred further inquiries to SGA adviser Charley Pride. Hurst apologised for the outburst and argued a censure required neglect of duties. All seven justices voted in favour of the censure.
src_label: Judicial Council emergency meeting minutes, 4 Feb 2018

title: Council dismissed a senator from the Senate
body: Meeting online, the Judicial Council dismissed Senator Annabelle Ford from the Senate for failing to answer the council, President Andi Dahmer or Speaker Ryan Richardson about repeated unexcused absences. The council had asked her a week earlier to state whether she had left SGA or would accept the consequences. It had recorded on 20 November 2017 that the Judicial Council could remove a person from a position while the Senate impeached.

title: Council censured a senator and ruled voting records public
body: The Judicial Council voted unanimously to censure Senator Dallas McKinney. On a request from student Jayden Thomas, who wanted senators' voting records viewable, it held that section 1.4 of the constitution required public records to be accessible to any member of student government and that section 2.6 of the bylaws could mean any official area such as the website or the SGA office. It also ruled that SGA could not endorse a candidate although other organisations could, and named Jacob McAndrews as the next chief justice with Lane Hedrick continuing as associate chief justice, both pending Senate approval.

title: On appeal the council reduced the disqualification to a suspension
body: Both disqualified campaigns appealed with the ten signatures that obliged the council to hear them. Chief Justice Annalicia Carlson abstained on the presidential ticket; Jacob McAndrews, Caroline Simpson and Isaac Keller voted to suspend the campaign and require an apology, Megan Armstrong and Lane Hedrick again to disqualify, so the suspension stood. The council voted unanimously to reinstate the McAvoy campaign. About sixty guests were recorded present, including a Herald reporter.

title: Two election code rulings in one emergency meeting
body: On a complaint about a stack of suggested senate candidates left at the Bates-Runner Hall desk, the council held 7-0 that there was no violation of election codes 3.4.1 or 3.4.3, because those govern posters, and none of 4.3.2, because each candidate had paid the full printing cost on their own sheet and a third party rather than the candidates had produced the endorsement. On a separate complaint supported by video, it held 7-0 that three posters on one floor of Grise Hall breached the two-per-floor rule and issued a verbal warning, the posters having already been removed.

title: Council defined a Senate majority as a majority of those present
body: At its first meeting of the year the council had to decide whether a majority in the Senate chamber was measured against those present or against the full membership. Chief Justice Isaac Keller argued that a senator who is not present abstains and loses the right to vote. No justice objected, and the council ruled unanimously that a simple majority is based on senators present.

title: Council ruled the Alpha Xi Delta resolution's clause constitutional 7-0
body: Asked by Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell to rule on the discrimination clause in Resolution 4-19-F, the council heard President Will Harris argue that defining discrimination was a Title IX matter rather than SGA's. All seven justices found the whereas clause constitutional, noting vagueness in section 1.1 and that SGA already awarded scholarships on protected characteristics. The ruling was made pending university information, and the council said a university finding of illegality would change it. The executive board vetoed the resolution 4-0 the next day.

title: Council convened a cross-branch rewrite of the constitution
body: Chief Justice Isaac Keller told the council that the executive and legislative branches wanted the constitution revamped to eliminate grey areas, and that three people from each branch would convene to work through changes. He said he would try to include the rest of the Judicial Council in the process.

title: Council refused a candidate an exemption to run for president
body: Joey Dilliha asked the council for an exemption under section 2.2.5 of the constitution to run for president without having held an elected or appointed SGA position. He said he had attended about three meetings as a freshman and had been occupied with internships and a business. Justices Erika Puhakka, Holden Schroeder, Jason Herlick, Turner Reynolds and Chief Justice Isaac Keller each said he was not familiar enough with the office and would be better suited to the Senate. The decision was unanimous, 5-0, that he could not run for president.

title: Council fixed the size of the Organizational Aid Board
body: Asked whether section 6.1.1's figure of six members for the Organizational Aid Board was a floor or a ceiling, the council ruled that six was the minimum needed for the board to operate and that the constitution set no maximum. At the same meeting it ruled that the executive vice president could appoint SGA senators to Faculty Senate committees.

title: Council ruled the constitution can be amended by ordinary bill
body: After debate on whether constitutional change required the special amendment committee, the council ruled that the constitution could be amended through bills, which students could write, and that the special committee was reserved for larger amendments. It also ruled that the constitution definitively placed the president on the Senate Executive Committee of Faculty Senate without a Senate confirmation.

title: Council held the constitution supreme over the bylaws on the executive veto
body: Ruling on a discrepancy between the constitution and the bylaws over which members of the executive cabinet could vote on a veto, the council held that supremacy went to the constitution and that the bylaws had to be amended to match. It took no action on votes already cast but required proper procedure in future. At the same meeting it set a standard of three unexcused committee-meeting absences for senators, effective the following semester, with no action against senators already over the line.

title: Council held college seats must be filled from their colleges
body: Answering questions from Senator Ethan Huffaker, the council held that college, transfer and class senate seats must be filled by students of that college, status or class, because the requirement is inherent in the name of the seat. It held that only the freshman, graduate, international and Gatton Academy seats become senator-at-large seats when vacant under section 3.8.2, and that all other named seats remain what they are even when unfilled.

title: Council ruled a constitutional amendment veto can be overridden by two thirds
body: Answering the Secretary of the Senate, the council held that a presidential veto of a constitutional amendment could be overridden by a two-thirds vote under section 3.1.9, that the veto power extended to bylaw amendments, that senators elected in spring take office in the fall and cannot conduct business before then, and that nothing in the governing documents stopped the Senate funding bills from outside the legislative discretionary line. It also granted amnesty on late election expenditure sheets.

title: Constitutional Referendum Committee began work
body: Chief Justice Isaac King told the council the Constitutional Referendum Committee would start on 14 February 2024 at 7pm. By 13 March the committee had written twelve bills, to be presented after spring break. The package that reached the Senate raised grade point floors, retitled the executive offices, required removal after a second censure in one year, and required a chief justice to be eligible to serve a full academic year.
src_label: Judicial Council minutes, 14 Feb and 13 Mar 2024

title: Council ruled a missed office hour counts as an unexcused absence
body: Under the heading of interpretation of the constitution and bylaws, the council decided that failure to complete office hours would be treated as an unexcused absence, so that two missed meetings and unfinished office hours amounted to three unexcused absences. Chief Justice Ellen Henderson had reported a large number of unsubmitted office hour forms and unexcused absences at the same meeting, and explained censure proceedings.

title: Council heard two candidates and nominated Blake Graham chief justice
body: After the spring elections the council heard speeches from two contenders for chief justice, deliberated and voted. Chief Justice Morgan Gammons recorded that the council would nominate Blake Graham for chief justice the following week, for confirmation by the Senate.

title: Council set its own attendance standard
body: Chief Justice Blake Graham recorded that senator attendance would now be judged on three criteria, timeliness, thoroughness and validity of the excuse, and that the council itself would meet permanently on Wednesdays at 6pm with a maximum of two unexcused absences, voting on each other's attendance with the justice in question recused. The council also set out a strategy for revising the constitution and said it aimed to join the appeals process for parking and transportation citations.

title: Council refused the executive cabinet's censure of a senator 7-0
body: President Rush Robinson, Vice President Savanna Kurtz, Chief Financial Officer Gabriel Jerdon, Chief of Staff Maggie Yelton, Speaker Hadley Whipple and Chief Communications Officer Preston Jenkins brought five charges against Senator Jade Ismail, covering inexact costs on bills, items left in the SGA office, pressuring the Senate by arranging events before their bills passed, marketing and negligence at an event. In a unanimous 7-0 decision the council declined to censure. Chief Justice Blake Graham's opinion struck the office-items charge, held that pressuring the Senate was not constitutionally defined and that the council was working on defining it, and encouraged but could not require two extra office hours spent in meetings with the officers concerned.

title: Council granted a unanimous eligibility exemption and lost a justice
body: Under section 2.2.5 a student who had not served a full year in SGA asked to run for executive office; the exemption required a unanimous vote, and the council granted it 6-0 after hearing the applicant. At the same meeting it ruled that family members could help campaign and that outside organisations could endorse tickets, provided no incentives were offered for showing votes. Associate Justice Kaden Blankenship resigned from the council effective 2 April 2026 and stood on a presidential ticket.

title: Council censured a presidential ticket during the election
body: Acting on its own initiative rather than a complaint, the council found the Marshall, Blankenship and VanRude ticket guilty 4-0 of breaching section 3.11 of the election codes, which barred distribution of perishable food within 48 hours of an election, after Red Bull cans were handed out at their table and a photograph was reposted to their campaign story. Chief Justice Sophie Stirling and Associate Chief Justice Hannah Hash held that the legal test for perishability was not open to debate and that ticket members were responsible for educating their campaign team. The council issued a formal censure but declined to remove the ticket from the ballot.

title: Council disbanded a campaign team and narrowed its own precedent
body: On an anonymous complaint of campaigning in the Commons while voting was open, backed by video the chief justice and associate chief justice obtained themselves, the council found the same ticket guilty 5-0 of breaching election codes 3.13 and 3.13.1 on polling places and not guilty on 3.6.8 on posters. It held that its precedent in Lee, Rosenbaum, Willmes v. Cook of fall 2025, which made a candidate wholly responsible for campaign materials, was too broad for acts by a team member, and narrowed it. It censured and disbanded the MBV campaign team rather than issuing the ticket a second censure, ruled that future breaches by designated team members would be attributable to the ticket, and required all tickets to file campaign team rosters before elections.

title: The Herald prints the constitution in full
body: The whole text of the constitution of the Associated Students filled page 8 of the College Heights Herald of 7 April 1966, six days after President Kelly Thompson approved it and three weeks before the ratification vote. Fourteen articles set out an executive of four elected officers, a Student Congress of twenty-five representative seats, a Judicial Council of seven, three constitutional committees and a Student Affairs Board. WKU Archives holds this printing as the copy of record.
src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Herald, 7 Apr 1966

title: The first Congress seats twenty-five
body: The roster of the first Congress of Associated Students, elected in May 1966, names twenty-five people: the four officers and twenty-one representatives. Three class councils sent their president, vice president and representative at large; the freshman seats are absent and only one of the two women's residence hall seats is filled. David Arvin, Forrest Lanning and Marshall Peace are marked as the three representatives on the Executive Council.
src_label: UA3/3/1 Congress of Associated Students roster, 1966

title: The first amendment goes on the ballot
body: The spring 1968 ballot carried a constitutional amendment beside the cheerleader vote and a fee question. It would have required a candidate for treasurer of the Associated Students to be an accounting or business major or minor with at least six credit hours of accounting including the current semester's work. The election results memo of 3 May 1968 reports the officer races and a turnout of 2,894 but does not record how the amendment was decided.
src_label: UA3/3/1 Student Election Ballot, April 1968; UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, 3 May 1968

title: Congress votes to reopen the constitution
body: At the meeting of 13 February 1969 Kent Gildersleeve introduced a resolution creating a Constitutional Revision Committee of no more than ten members, three elected by and from Congress and seven appointed by the president of the Associated Students, one of them from the Executive Council and one from the Judicial Council. It passed, and Congress elected Gildersleeve, Mike Durham and Doug Alexander. The Herald reported the vote the following week as 18 to 1 to re-examine the constitution. The archive's existing 27 February 1969 entry refers to the same committee.
src_label: SGA Meeting Minutes, 13 Feb 1969; Herald 48:18, 20 Feb 1969

title: Four amendments go to students
body: Congress moved on 24 April 1970 to seek ratification of four changes to the constitution. The Herald of 1 May reported voting continuing until 4 p.m. that day for cheerleaders and amendments. The article index does not record what the four changes were or how they were decided.

title: A quorum question is put on the ballot
body: The Herald of 2 October 1970 reported that voters would decide a constitutional quorum question for the Associated Student Congress in the following Tuesday's balloting, in the same issue that recorded a primary turnout of 8.9 per cent. The 1966 constitution required two-thirds of Congress's total membership to be present for business. The record does not give the result.

title: A new constitution passes, 1,397 to 697
body: Students approved a new Associated Students constitution on 10 December 1970 by roughly two to one, 1,397 yes to 697 no, with 2,094 voting. President John Lyne put turnout at about 23 per cent of eligible voters. The Rules and Elections Committee, which normally ran campus elections, had refused to supervise the referendum on the grounds that its members were too involved in end-of-semester activities, so a committee under Cathy Ashabraner ran it with paper ballots and announced the result before a basketball game. The document called for a student code of rights, a strengthened judicial system, a second vice president for entertainment, a restructured Congress and more financial autonomy. It was to go to the administration and then the Board of Regents; the Herald said the administration had hinted it might face rough sledding.

title: The revision committee reports
body: The Herald of 3 September 1971 reported the constitution revisers completing their final document, and on 21 September that the Constitution Revision Committee had released its findings. The work had been running since a panel opened a study in February 1971, ten months after the December 1970 referendum. The article index carries the headlines and not the text.

title: Congress approves the new constitution
body: Congress approved the revised constitution on 3 March 1972, after voting section by section: it took up a section on 22 February and accepted the executive branch on 29 February, the Herald printing the proposed executive article alongside the vote.

title: 157 to 16, on a turnout under two per cent
body: The two-day constitutional referendum ran on 29 and 30 March 1972. The vote was 157 for and 16 against, 90 per cent in favour, with a simple majority required to pass. Fewer than two per cent of Western's 10,133 students voted. The new constitution renamed the organisation the Associated Student Government, created an administrative vice presidency and an activities and programs vice presidency in place of the single vice president, rebuilt Congress on ten representatives-at-large plus two from each academic college, removed the Interfraternity, Panhellenic, residence hall, general club and honor group seats, and revised the judicial branch. The Herald called it the culmination of eighteen months of deliberation by two bodies of Congress.

title: The 1972 constitution takes effect
body: The constitution ratified in March 1972 became effective immediately after the installation of the new officers of the Associated Student Government, scheduled for 27 April 1972. Filing for the newly created offices opened on 31 March. From that date the body's name was the Associated Student Government.

title: Constitutional abuses alleged against an officer
body: The Herald of 3 October 1975 carried a report by Jay Wethington and Roger Harris headed with allegations of constitutional abuses against Rick Kelley, the activities vice president who chaired the Student Activities Committee. The surviving index records the allegation and no resolution; the archive holds no report of an outcome.

title: Bill 11 sends the revision to the students
body: Congress had created a Constitutional Revision Committee by Bill 2 on 7 September 1976. On 5 April 1977 it passed Bill 11, to hold a referendum on the proposed constitutional revisions. President Christy Vogt's closing letter of 26 April 1977 left constitutional revision as the first of four items she recommended to the administration, and the Herald reported in September 1977 that the organisation was still awaiting approval of the changes.
src_label: SGA Bill 11 - Forward Constitutional Revision, 5 Apr 1977

title: Congress passes constitutional amendments
body: Tom Beshear reported in the Herald of 8 February 1979 that the Associated Student Government had passed constitution amendments, ten weeks after the congress approved a revised constitution on 30 November 1978. The index preserves the headline and not the substance.

title: By-laws amended on expelling representatives
body: Bill 86-31-S, passed on 8 April 1986, amended the by-laws on the expulsion of representatives, tied to attendance at the Academic Council. It came in the same spring as Bill 86-19-S on college representative voting, Bill 86-21-S adopting a new membership application, Bill 86-9-S on campaign regulations and Bill 86-8-S amending the by-laws.
src_label: SGA Bill 86-31-S - Amendment of By-Laws for Expulsion of Representatives

title: An impeachment begun and dropped
body: Jill Duff reported on 19 November 1987 that the student government had begun impeachment proceedings against Bill Schilling. On 3 December 1987 the Herald reported the request for impeachment dropped. Schilling had sat on the Judicial Council in 1986-87, and the Herald of 11 December 1986 had reported that one member wrote most of the congress's bills, naming him.

title: Two resolutions to amend the constitution
body: In the spring 1991 session the Associated Student Government passed Resolution 91-19-S, proposals for constitutional amendments, and Resolution 91-20-S, an amendment to Article IV on the judicial branch. They came alongside the run of by-law bills 91-4-S, 91-5-S and 91-6-S, the last of which changed the procedure for overriding a presidential veto. The day of these items is not recorded in the archive.

title: Bill 02-07-F amended the bylaws of finance
body: SGA's own legislation archive dates Bill 02-07-F, an Amendment to the By-Laws of Finance of the Student Government Association, to 11 October 2002. It was passed in the same weeks as the dispute over unaccounted-for SGA money, and the Spring 2005 bylaws later named it as the rule the association's chief financial officer had to follow.
src_label: WKU SGA legislation archive, 2002 (Wayback capture, 21 Jan 2004)

title: Bill 03-10-F brought a new constitution and bylaws to Congress
body: Robert Watkins, chair of the Legislative Research Committee, wrote the documents in the autumn of 2003 after reviewing constitutions from other universities, among them 23 he consulted on the chief of staff post alone. SGA's legislation archive dates Bill 03-10-F, New Constitution and Bylaws, to 10 November 2003; the Herald reported the first reading on 11 November.

title: Judicial Council adopted the 2004 Election Codes
body: The codes, adopted 22 January 2004, gave the Judicial Council supervision of all elections, set filing between 1 February and 2 March, made a 17 February candidate orientation compulsory on pain of disqualification, and capped campaign spending at $450 for president, $400 for executive vice president, $350 for other executive offices and $50 for legislative candidates. Appeals had to be filed within three business days of the results.

title: Congress passed the new constitution at the fifth attempt
body: SGA congress unanimously approved a new constitution and set of bylaws on 10 February 2004. Four earlier attempts had failed because the two-thirds of congress needed to vote on legislation was not present. Twenty-five of twenty-nine congress members were there, against 75 seats allowed under the old constitution; new members had been sworn in and about thirteen who had missed more than three meetings had been removed from the roll by the judicial council in the preceding fortnight. Watkins called the delay disturbing and said it showed why a new system was needed.

title: 132 students ratified the new constitution, 116 to 16
body: Voting ran on TopNet from 12:01 a.m. to 11:59 p.m. on 9 March 2004. The constitution and bylaws were approved by 116 students with 16 against and no abstentions, out of 132 votes cast; about 18,000 students had been enrolled the previous semester. The changes took effect the following semester. Associate justice Dana Lockhart noted that seats left open could still be filled by appointment rather than election under the new document.

title: Nine candidates stood for 28 spring senate seats
body: With the referendum still to be counted, nine students had filed for the legislative seats to be elected on 16 and 17 March: Melissa Paris, Katharine Pettit, Brittany Fausey, John Law, Alicia Bachicha, Abby Lovan, Sarah Cecil, Mason Stevenson and Robert Watkins. The proposed senate had 35 seats, 28 of them elected in the spring. President John Bradley said the judicial council would decide the next year how to fill positions with no candidates.

title: SGA published the Spring 2005 documents as its governing texts
body: The documents page of SGA's website linked its Constitution and Bylaws to files headed "SGA Constitution as Proposed Spring 2005" and "SGA Bylaws as Proposed for Spring 2005." The date given is the Internet Archive capture; the page itself carried none. It is the clearest surviving evidence of which text governed the association after the March 2005 referendum.

title: Grade point average amendment fails
body: The College Heights Herald of 9 February 2016, volume 91 number 5, carried an item indexed as "Grade Point Average Amendment Fails in Student Government Association." The 4 February issue, volume 91 number 4, carried an item indexed as "Student Government Association Passes Changes to Current Bylaws." The index gives the headlines only; the archive holds no fuller account of either vote.

title: Senate merges the Academic Affairs and Student Affairs committees
body: Bill 28-17-S, first reading 18 April and second reading 25 April 2017, passed 28-0-0. It replaced sections 5.3 and 5.4 with a single Academic and Student Affairs Committee serving the student body on all non-academic and academic affairs, on the stated ground that the two overlapped on scholarship work and that the Student Affairs duty to address cultural issues had passed to MyCampusToo. The constitution WKU posted as amended spring 2017 still lists the two committees separately.

title: Bill 8-20-S puts emergency clauses to the Senate
body: With campus closed by COVID-19, Bill 8-20-S had its first reading on 14 April 2020. Authored by Dawson McCoun and MJ Mayo, it provided that on a two-thirds Senate vote together with a majority of the Executive Cabinet and a majority of the Judicial Council, officers and senators could extend their terms until a new election was held, the president could extend the student regent position under KRS 164.321, and the rescheduled election would be held within three weeks of the start of the fall 2020 semester. The clause as later printed in the constitution allows four weeks and adds virtual Senate meetings.

title: A constitutional amendment passes 31-0 and is vetoed the same day
body: Bill 13-22-S, redefining the duties of the Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee around a holistic approach to wellness, was first read on 15 February 2022 and given a second reading on 22 February. The bill sheet records an initial Senate vote of 31 pass and 0 fail and a veto on 22 February 2022. A revised version, Bill 22-22-S, carrying shorter wording, was first read on 8 March and passed on 22 March.

title: Judicial Council gets its first written procedural rules
body: Bill 17-22-S, first read 1 March 2022 and given a second reading on 8 March, supported adoption of the General Procedural Rules of the Judicial Council. The bill stated that the council had previously had no formal written established guidelines or procedures pertaining to its functions and duties. The rules that followed rank as equal to the Legislative Bylaws, set out the council's attendance, censure and judicial review procedure, and provide for the Senate to override a Judicial Council veto by two-thirds of those present and voting.

title: Community Relations Committee added to the constitution
body: Bill 21-22-S, first read 8 March 2022 and given a second reading on 22 March, amended the constitution to establish a Community Relations Committee to advocate for students' needs in Bowling Green, coordinate volunteer service and run a yearly voter drive. The bill stated the committee was not meant for pushing a political agenda. Its authors were senators Margaret Glaser, Emily Bunning and Cole Bornefeld.

title: Senate lowers the bar for changing its own constitution
body: Bill 22-24-S, one of the package given a second reading on 28 March 2024, amended clause 10.1 so that the constitution may be amended by a two-thirds vote of the present senators rather than of the full membership of the Senate. The bill stated that the old rule limited amendment votes to meetings at which at least two-thirds of the full Senate were in attendance. Bill 23-24-S, passed the same night, moved constitutional amendment elections from the end of the fall and spring semesters to the fall and spring senator elections, citing higher turnout in representative elections.
